transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. Can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, I'm here because I just feel like I don't deserve the trust people put in me right now. I'm a physician, and lately, I just keep replaying these really small clinical imperfections in my head... and I look at them as if they prove I'm a dangerous doctor. It's just been really weighing on me.
Did these thoughts start after a particular incident or stressful event at work, such as a specific mistake or patient outcome, or have they developed gradually over time without a clear trigger?
No, it wasn't a bad patient outcome or a specific mistake. It's actually been going on for about a year and a month now. And, um, it started right after I received a clinic award, actually.
Over this past year, have you noticed a persistent low or depressed mood, or a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, most of the day nearly every day?

Yeah, definitely. Um, especially the loss of interest part. I used to do a lot outside of work—I would plan weekend hikes, go out to take sunrise photos, or cook these big Indonesian dinners for my friends. But for months now, I just haven't wanted to. All those things just feel like heavy obligations, and I... I just can't make myself care about them anymore.

When you replay these clinical imperfections in your mind, do they feel like intrusive, unwanted thoughts that push you to do something—like double-checking charts, seeking reassurance, or mentally reviewing cases—to make the anxiety go away?

Um, no, I wouldn't say it's like that. I don't feel pushed to go back and double-check charts or ask my colleagues for reassurance to make myself feel better. It's not really about trying to make the anxiety go away. I just... I just dwell on those moments and feel completely convinced that I'm doing harm. I don't do anything to try to fix it, I just sort of sit with the feeling that I'm a danger to my patients.
Before this past year, have you ever had a similar period—lasting weeks or more—where you felt this kind of persistent low mood or loss of interest?

No, I don't think so. Before this started last year, I never really had a time where I felt this low or just stopped caring about my hobbies for weeks at a time. This is... this is the first time it's been like this.

Along with the low mood and loss of interest, have you noticed changes in your sleep or appetite—such as sleeping much more or less than usual, or a significant change in your eating—over this past year?

Um, no, I haven't really noticed any big changes there. My sleep has been pretty normal, I think. I haven't been sleeping a lot more or less than I usually do. And my appetite is about the same, too. I'm still eating my normal meals, not really eating more or less than before. So, no, nothing like that.

When colleagues or objective evidence show you that your patient care was actually fine, are you able to consider that they might be right, or does part of you remain completely convinced you're causing harm no matter what anyone says?

I just... I remain completely convinced I'm causing harm. It doesn't matter what anyone says. Even when I go back and review the chart myself, and there's absolutely no evidence of a bad outcome... I just keep believing that some routine delay, or some imperfect message I sent, has quietly harmed a patient. I just know that everyone is eventually going to discover it.
Over this past year, have you noticed a persistent lack of energy or feeling unusually fatigued, even when you haven't been physically exerting yourself?

No, not really. My energy levels have been pretty normal, actually. I mean, I get tired after a long shift, but I haven't noticed any unusual fatigue or just feeling drained for no reason. So, no, my energy is mostly fine.
Given how convinced you feel about causing harm, have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself or that you don't deserve to keep living?

I don't have a plan to kill myself or anything. But... I do catch myself thinking that it might be better if I just didn't wake up. Especially after a day when I'm really convinced I've let my patients down. It just feels like things would be easier, but no, I don't have an actual plan to hurt myself.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a single, continuous 13-month episode of depressed mood and marked anhedonia (loss of interest in previously enjoyed hobbies), meeting core criteria for a major depressive episode. Superimposed on this is a mood-congruent delusional belief—an unshakeable, evidence-resistant conviction that he is a dangerous physician causing harm to patients—which is not accompanied by compulsive checking/reassurance-seeking behaviors, ruling out OCD. The delusion is fixed and not modifiable by objective evidence, distinguishing it from an obsession, and its content (guilt, worthlessness, deserving punishment) is congruent with depressive themes rather than a primary psychotic disorder (which would not require a preceding/co-occurring depressive syndrome). There is no history of prior depressive or manic episodes, confirming this is a single episode. Passive suicidal ideation without plan is present, consistent with severity. The combination of a major depressive episode with mood-congruent psychotic (delusional) features supports F32.3 as the primary diagnosis, with delusional disorder (F22) and OCD (F42.9) considered and reasonably excluded.
